say.text: Two stems look alike. Here is the first: which groin hernia is most likely to strangulate?

choices.label: Direct inguinal hernia, medial to the vessels
Femoral hernia, below the inguinal ligament
Indirect inguinal hernia, lateral to the vessels
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: 'Groin' is a wider word than 'inguinal'. Count every groin type, then ask which one has the narrowest neck.
Yes. Among groin hernias, femoral carries the highest risk of strangulation.
'Groin' takes in femoral, so the groin ranking differs from the inguinal one.
Not quite. A direct sac is tempting because it bulges broadly and looks dangerous.
But a direct hernia has a wide neck and is the classic answer for one that rarely strangulates. Femoral is the riskiest groin type.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the rule: risk follows the neck, not the bulk.

say.text: Not quite. Indirect is tempting: it is the commonest inguinal type, and 'groin' sounds like the canal.
But the question says groin, which adds femoral. Femoral has the highest strangulation risk of the groin hernias.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read the scope word every time. Groin is wider than inguinal.

say.text: Same question, narrower stem, with femoral left out: which inguinal hernia is most likely to strangulate?

choices.label: Direct inguinal hernia, with a wide neck
Indirect inguinal hernia, through the deep ring
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Bulk is not the test here. Ask which inguinal sac has the narrower neck at its entrance.
Yes. Indirect has a narrow neck at the deep ring, so its contents can be gripped and strangulated.
Between the two inguinal types, it is the one more liable to strangulate.
Not quite. Direct looks the riskier sac because it bulges broadly.
But its neck is wide, and it is the classic answer for the hernia that rarely strangulates.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Wide and bulky feels dangerous, but the test is the neck.

say.text: Not quite. Pantaloon looks bulkier, so it feels riskier, and bulk is what tempts you here.
Risk follows the neck, not the total bulk. The indirect neck is the narrow one that grips.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Bulk tempts; the neck decides.

say.text: Why is the indirect hernia more liable to strangulate than the direct one?

choices.label: A wide neck lets more bowel slide into the sac each time
A narrow neck at the deep ring constricts the bowel loop
Its larger bulge pushes on the vessels, cutting supply
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Strangulation is a supply problem. Ask what happens to the blood when a loop is squeezed at the entrance.
Yes. A narrow neck grips the contents. Venous return is obstructed first, then arterial supply fails.
Gangrene follows that sequence, so the sequence, not the size of the swelling, sets the urgency.
Not quite. A wide-necked sac seems to hold more bowel, so it feels more dangerous.
The neck sets the grip, and a wide neck grips least. The direct hernia has that wide neck and rarely strangulates.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Hold the picture: wide neck, weak grip; narrow neck, strong grip.

say.text: Not quite. A bigger bulge seems to squeeze the vessels, so bulk looks like the danger.
The danger sits at the neck. The constriction, not the bulge, cuts the supply.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Bulk does not predict strangulation; the neck does.

say.text: An elderly woman has a tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, with vomiting. Most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Strangulated indirect inguinal hernia, through the deep ring
Strangulated femoral hernia, through the femoral canal
Strangulated direct inguinal hernia, through Hesselbach's triangle
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with where the lump sits relative to the pubic tubercle, then ask which groin type sits there.
Yes. An inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle; femoral lies below and lateral.
Femoral is also the groin type with the highest strangulation risk.
Not quite. Indirect is tempting because it is the commonest groin type and the one you picture first.
But this lump lies below and lateral to the tubercle, which is femoral territory, and femoral strangulates most.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Position decides the type before commonness does.

say.text: Not quite. A direct sac is tempting because its bulge sits in the same groin area.
But direct lies above and medial to the tubercle, through Hesselbach's triangle. This lump is below and lateral.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Check position against the tubercle before you pick the type.

say.text: Which hernia is the most common in women?

choices.label: Femoral hernia, relatively commoner in women
Indirect inguinal hernia, from the deep ring
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Read the question's words. Does 'most common' rank types within women, or compare women with men?
Yes. Indirect inguinal is the most common hernia in women, and in both sexes overall.
Not quite. Femoral is tempting because it is relatively more common in women than in men.
That is a comparison across the sexes. Within women, indirect still leads.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Relatively more is not most common; keep the qualifier.

say.text: Pick the true statement about sex and hernia type.

choices.label: Femoral outnumbers the inguinal types among women
Inguinal hernia is much commoner in women than in men
Femoral is relatively commoner in women, yet indirect leads

say.text: Yes. Femoral is relatively commoner in women, but indirect is still the most common in women.
'Relatively' compares the sexes, and 'most common' ranks the types.
Not quite. Femoral is the sex-skew hernia, so it looks like the female leader.
It does not outnumber all the inguinal types. Indirect is still the commonest in women.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Read 'relatively' as a comparison, not a rank.

say.text: Not quite. The sex skew tempts you to flip the sexes, so inguinal seems commoner in women.
Inguinal hernia is far more common in males. Its commonest type in women is still indirect.

sure_note.text: You were sure. The sex gap for inguinal hernia runs the other way.

say.text: A tense, tender, irreducible groin swelling with no cough impulse, vomiting, and a toxic patient. Your first step?

choices.label: Attempt gentle, then firm, manual reduction
Resuscitate and take to emergency surgery
Request an ultrasound of the groin first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Before any reduction, decide one thing about the bowel: is it still alive?
Yes. A strangulated hernia needs emergency surgery, with resection of any non-viable bowel.
Its picture is tense, tender and irreducible, with no cough impulse.
Not quite. Reducing first is the reducible-hernia habit, and it feels like the quick, kind move.
With strangulation, forceful taxis can push dead bowel back or reduce it en masse. Viability is decided first.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so treat strangulation signs as the signal to stop reducing.

say.text: Not quite. A scan feels thorough, so an investigation seems the sensible first move.
Ultrasound is for an occult or uncertain swelling. A strangulated hernia needs theatre, not a scan.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Match the test to the question; here the question is an emergency.

say.text: Why is forceful reduction avoided when strangulation is suspected?

choices.label: It turns the hernia into an irreducible, fixed swelling
It can push dead bowel back or cause en masse reduction
It is allowed once analgesia has been given in full

say.text: Yes. Taxis can push gangrenous bowel back, or reduce sac and contents together.
In reduction en masse the constriction persists under the skin, so the bowel stays at risk.
Not quite. The fear is that reduction makes the hernia stuck, so it sounds like the reason to avoid it.
The real hazard is the bowel: gangrenous loops are pushed back, or the constriction persists.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Taxis is avoided for the bowel's state, not the hernia's.

say.text: Not quite. Analgesia makes the patient comfortable, so it can seem to make reduction safe.
Comfort does not change the bowel. Forceful reduction is avoided in strangulation regardless of pain relief.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Pain relief is not the test; viability is.

say.text: Now a visible, reducible groin swelling with an expansile cough impulse, in a fit man. Your next step?

choices.label: Ultrasound of the groin before any surgery
Plan elective repair; imaging is not needed
CT of the abdomen and pelvis before surgery

say.text: Yes. A clinically evident hernia is a clinical diagnosis, so imaging adds nothing to the decision.
Scans are kept for an occult hernia or a complicated presentation.
Not quite. Ultrasound feels safe before an operation, so it seems a sensible check.
It is for an uncertain or occult lump. This swelling is visible, so the scan adds delay, not a decision.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Match the test to whether the hernia is visible.

say.text: Not quite. CT looks thorough, so the most advanced test seems the safest choice.
CT is kept for complicated or obscure presentations, not a visible, reducible lump.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Most advanced is not most useful; it is the question that decides.

say.text: What is the investigation of choice for an occult groin hernia?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: 'Occult' means hidden on examination. Which test is the first look for a hidden hernia, before anything more advanced?
Yes. Ultrasonography is the first imaging test for an occult hernia.
If ultrasound is inconclusive, MRI is the more sensitive next step.
Not quite. CT looks like the most complete test, so it feels right for a hidden lump.
CT is kept for complicated or obscure presentations. For an occult hernia, ultrasound comes first.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Most complete is not most useful first; ultrasound is.

say.text: Not quite. Herniography is a hernia test by name, so it sounds like the specific answer.
It is historical and has been largely replaced by cross-sectional imaging.

sure_note.text: You were sure. A test named after the hernia is not automatically the right one.

say.text: An appendix lies inside a femoral hernia sac. Which eponym?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Both eponyms hold an appendix. What separates them is the site, and this stem names the site.
Yes. De Garengeot hernia is the appendix within a femoral sac.
Not quite. Amyand's is the better-known appendix hernia, so it comes to mind first.
But Amyand's is the inguinal one: the appendix within an inguinal sac. The femoral sac is de Garengeot's.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Anchor each eponym to its site, not only to the organ.

say.text: At surgery for an inguinal hernia, the surgeon finds an inflamed appendix in the sac. Which eponym?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Same organ, different site. Which eponym is tied to the inguinal sac?
Yes. Amyand's is the appendix within an inguinal sac.
The matching set also includes Littre's, Richter's and Maydl's, so learn each with its site or content.
Not quite. De Garengeot is also an appendix hernia, which is why it tempts you.
But it is the femoral sac. This sac is inguinal, so the answer is Amyand's.

sure_note.text: You were sure. Same organ, different site: the site picks the eponym.

say.text: Three words to carry: neck, scope, site.
Neck: a narrow neck at the deep ring grips the bowel, so the indirect type strangulates more.
Scope: groin takes in femoral, which carries the highest strangulation risk of the groin types.
